title: Yara and the Atlas
premise: In the final year of the Great War, Jonah Galloway, driver and letter-reader for prominent suffragist Edith Marchmont, has built a life on knowing which secrets to keep. When an infant is abandoned at the Marchmont house with a note instructing the finder to forget its face, Jonah recognizes the handwriting as belonging to a woman who vanished from Edith's circle years ago — a woman whose disappearance is tangled in Edith's own past and in letters Jonah was never meant to keep. As the armistice negotiations race toward conclusion, Jonah must choose between the loyalty that has defined them and the truth that history is already being written without, racing to get the record straight before the victors' historians seal it. In the end, Jonah delivers the last letter — the one that names the child, the mother, and Edith's complicity — and chooses a visible life, keeping the child rather than the silence.
about_author: Tamsin Montrose is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing private letters in country-house collections before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted coach house in Yorkshire, where she remains professionally unable to resist reading other people's post.

chapters.title: The Weight of Other People's Words
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Establishes Jonah's twelve years as Edith Marchmont's driver and unofficial reader of her correspondence, the war grinding on, and the careful art of knowing which silences keep people safe. Emotional beat: the comfort and quiet loneliness of invisibility.

chapters.title: A Bundle at the Door
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. On a freezing November night, an infant is left on the Marchmont doorstep with a note: 'Forget the face.' Jonah recognizes the handwriting instantly — Vera Ashworth, a woman who vanished from Edith's circle in 1912. Emotional beat: shock cracking open an ordered life.

chapters.title: What Mrs. Marchmont Does Not Ask
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith sees the child and, uncharacteristically, asks nothing — instructing Jonah to arrange care through the parish and say no more. Her evasion is itself a revelation. Emotional beat: the first hairline crack in Jonah's reverence for her employer.

chapters.title: Letters I Should Have Burned
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Going through the letter room, Jonah finds three letters from Vera that were never delivered — letters Edith ordered held. They hint at a scandal Edith buried to protect the suffrage movement's reputation. Emotional beat: complicity dawning.

chapters.title: The Child Who Has No Name
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, with interludes of the parish nurse. The baby, temporarily 'Infant Ashworth' on a register, is placed with a widow two lanes over; Jonah visits daily under the pretext of deliveries and begins, dangerously, to love her. Emotional beat: tenderness as risk.

chapters.title: An Old Address in Camden
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. On a delivery run to London, Jonah detours to Vera's last known address and finds a landlady who remembers Vera leaving in haste, pregnant, 'with a gentleman's card in her glove.' Emotional beat: the past acquiring a body and a voice.

chapters.title: The Gentleman's Card
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Flashback chapter to 1912: Vera's affair with a married MP whose patronage the movement depended upon, and Edith's cold arithmetic — silence the woman, save the cause. Emotional beat: sympathy for Edith that does not excuse her.

chapters.title: Someone Is Reading Over My Shoulder
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah notices letters re-ordered, a drawer re-locked, and realizes Edith suspects the held letters are found — or that someone else in the house, the new secretary Mr. Pell, is reporting. Emotional beat: surveillance and paranoia.

chapters.title: Mr. Pell's Efficient Hands
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. The secretary, ambitious and connected to the MP's family, is quietly gathering material to protect his patron's postwar legacy — including any record of Vera. Emotional beat: the enemy revealed as a historian of the victors in miniature.

chapters.title: Armistice Rumors
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Peace feels imminent; newspapers speak of how the war will be remembered and by whom. Jonah understands that once the guns stop, no one will want an old scandal reopened. Emotional beat: the clock beginning to run.

chapters.title: The Widow's Question
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The foster widow, growing attached, asks Jonah plainly whether the child has family — because a gentleman's solicitor has been asking after 'a foundling of quality.' Emotional beat: the child becoming a contested object.

chapters.title: Vera, Alive
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A trail — a pawn ticket, a hospital record — leads Jonah to a convalescent home where Vera Ashworth is dying of the influenza's long tail. She gives Jonah her account and a final letter naming the father. Emotional beat: grief and urgency braided together.

chapters.title: The Letter I Was Told to Forget
chapters.summary: Vera's POV (her deathbed recollection). Vera's version of 1912: the promises, the exile, the child she could not raise, and her instruction to 'forget the face' — a mother's protection, not a command to erase. Emotional beat: reframing the whole story.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Green Room
chapters.summary: Jonah and Edith, alternating. Jonah lays the letters on Edith's desk and demands the truth go on record. Edith, cornered, admits everything but argues the record will destroy the movement's fragile gains. Emotional beat: loyalty and truth finally at open war.

chapters.title: What Pell Steals
chapters.summary: Pell's POV. Pell takes Vera's final letter and the held correspondence, intending to deliver them to the MP's family before the armistice makes them worthless — or dangerous. Emotional beat: violation; the record itself under threat.

chapters.title: The Long Drive North
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah pursues Pell's motorcar through a November storm to intercept the handoff, a chase that doubles as a reckoning with every mile Jonah has driven in silence. Emotional beat: the invisible man made visible at last.

chapters.title: The House of the Gentleman
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At the MP's estate, Jonah confronts the family — and finds the MP himself, broken by the war's losses, willing to acknowledge the child if the truth is told properly, not blackmailed. Emotional beat: unexpected humanity in the enemy's house.

chapters.title: Armistice Eve
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, multiple POVs. Bells are expected at any hour; Edith must decide whether to sign a sanitized account for the movement's official history, and Jonah must decide what to do with the recovered letters. Emotional beat: everything balanced on a knife's edge.

chapters.title: The Bells and the Burning
chapters.summary: Climax. Jonah's POV. As armistice bells ring, Edith burns the official draft and, in a final act of courage, dictates a true deposition for Jonah to carry to the record office — while Pell, exposed, is dismissed and his copies surrendered. Emotional beat: catharsis; truth winning at cost.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah delivers the deposition, Vera's letter, and the naming of the child to the county archive, insisting on their own name as witness — the first time in twelve years Jonah has asked to be remembered. Emotional beat: claiming a self.

chapters.title: A Name for the Child
chapters.summary: Jonah and Edith, shared scene. The child is christened Vera Marchmont Galloway, with Edith as godmother and Jonah as guardian; the MP's family sends, at last, an honest letter. Emotional beat: belonging forged rather than inherited.

chapters.title: The Driver Who Reads No More Letters
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, epilogue. Spring 1919: Jonah keeps the motorcar but opens a letter-writing service for families of the fallen, putting ordinary truths on record. The child sleeps in the basket beside the seat where she was once abandoned. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace.
